Deep Space Mission · Launch 2031

There is an ocean
under the ice.

AETHELON is a robotic mission to Enceladus — Saturn's smallest round moon, hiding a global liquid-water ocean beneath a shell of ice. Scroll to follow the seven-year journey.

Trace the trajectory → Explore the system
Stage 01 · Departure

Leaving Earth at 11.2 km/s

AETHELON breaks free of Earth's gravity well and begins a looping inner-system cruise, borrowing speed from the planets instead of carrying the fuel to do it alone.

Stage 02 · Gravity Assist

A slingshot past Venus

Diving toward the Sun, the probe whips around Venus. The flyby bends its path and adds tens of kilometres per second — for free — flinging it back outward.

Stage 03 · Outbound Cruise

Six years across the dark

Past the asteroid belt and a Jupiter assist, AETHELON coasts through the outer Solar System, instruments asleep, drinking power from its radioisotope generator.

Stage 04 · Arrival

Saturn orbit insertion

A 96-minute engine burn captures the probe into Saturn's grip. Ahead lies Enceladus — and the first close look at the geysers feeding the rings.

The question

Could life begin in an alien sea?

In 2005 the Cassini spacecraft flew through a curtain of icy spray erupting from Enceladus' south pole and tasted it: water vapour, salt, silica nanograins, and complex organic molecules. The plumes are the moon's hidden ocean, venting into space. AETHELON's single purpose is to fly back through those geysers — slower, closer, and with instruments a generation sharper — and ask whether anything in that water is alive.

A crowded neighbourhood

Enceladus rides Saturn's E-ring

Enceladus orbits Saturn every 33 hours, locked in a 2:1 resonance with neighbouring Dione that flexes its interior and keeps the ocean liquid. Its geysers don't just escape — they paint the entire E-ring, the faint blue band that arcs across Saturn's sky. AETHELON threads this system, using each moon's gravity to refine its approach.

  • Enceladus — prime objective, ocean world
  • Tethys — pure-ice, imaged on approach
  • Dione — resonance partner, survey target
  • Titan — gravity-assist flybys

Payload

Tasting a geyser at four kilometres a second

AETHELON's core instrument is a high-resolution mass spectrometer that captures plume grains as the probe flies through them. At 4 km/s, every droplet hits the detector hard enough to shatter into its molecular fingerprint — letting scientists weigh amino acids, fatty acids and the chemistry of the ocean below, without ever landing.

  • Mass range to 2,000 Da — large organics resolved
  • Slow flythroughs preserve fragile molecules intact
  • Dust analyser sizes and counts every grain
  • Sub-surface radar sounds the ice shell thickness

Engineered for the cold and dark

A spacecraft built for one ocean.

Radioisotope power

At ten times Earth's distance from the Sun, solar panels are useless. A next-generation eMMRTG converts the heat of decaying plutonium-238 into 290 watts of steady electricity for two decades.

Autonomous flybys

A 78-minute light delay makes joysticking impossible. Onboard fault protection and optical navigation let AETHELON aim itself through each plume and recover from glitches alone.

Planetary protection

To keep an ocean that might host life pristine, the probe is sterilised to Category III standards and its end-of-mission disposal is plotted to never contaminate Enceladus.
